Parse dplyr's with_order(order_by, fun, x, ...) (what order_by() is)

Source: R/ir.R
ir_parse_with_order.Rd

dplyr 1.2.1: with_order(o, f, a1, ...) evaluates a1 and ... in ROW order, permutes only a1 into o order (stable, NA last), calls f(a1[perm], ...) and permutes the result back. Hence:

  • the windows f itself builds (a plain cumsum, or the cumsum()/row_number() of cummean(), the lag() of consecutive_id(), ...) run in o order: each gets meta$order_override;

  • windows inside a1 run in row order and get no override;

  • an elementwise f whose other arguments are all scalar literals is the plain row-order value (permutation commutes with it);

  • an elementwise f with another row-sized argument gives f(a1, b[inverse perm]), which has no native form: NULL.

Everything dplyr rejects (no a1, a scalar a1, an aggregate f, a name with_order() would capture) and everything the frame cannot do exactly (row_number(x)/ntile(x) tie-breaking by the order, first/last/nth, a nested order_by()) returns NULL, so the verb's whole-call CPU fallback gives dplyr's value or error: never an unordered native result.

Usage

ir_parse_with_order(order_ref, head, a1, rest, env, schema)

Arguments

order_ref

list(col =, desc =) from ir_parse_order_ref()

head

The raw expression of f (a symbol or pkg::sym)

a1

The raw expression of the permuted first argument

rest

Named list of the raw remaining arguments (none may read a column, and each must evaluate to a non-NULL atomic vector of length 1)

env

The environment the expressions are evaluated in

schema

The input schema (names, types)

Value

An IR node, or NULL

Details

Every user sub-expression is evaluated at most once, in dplyr's order: the first argument, then the others. The first argument is parsed once; when it is not a plain column, f is parsed over a placeholder column of the argument's type (and zone), the order is applied to that tree, and the argument's IR then replaces the placeholder. A re-parse of the raw argument would run a column-free call inside it (cumsum(x + runif(1))) again and build the IR from the second value.
